cases.title: Orientation: First Day at the Desk
cases.tagline: Three warm-up queries. Learn the editor, the schema explorer and how verdicts work.
brief: Welcome, Lead Data Auditor. Every case gives you a dossier, a real-world database and a list of findings to prove.
Write SQL in the editor, press Ctrl+Enter, and the engine tells you instantly how close you are - without revealing the answer.
Finish these three to unlock your first real case.

levels.title: Open the file
levels.story: Every audit starts by looking at the raw data. Run the starter query with Ctrl+Enter (or the RUN button).
levels.task: Show the first 5 rounds of funding_rounds, all columns, ordered by round_id.
hints: SELECT * returns every column.
ORDER BY round_id, then LIMIT 5.
SELECT * FROM funding_rounds ORDER BY round_id LIMIT 5;

levels.title: Filter the big cheques
levels.story: Big rounds make headlines. Pull them out.
levels.task: List startup and amount_usd for rounds of at least 50,000,000 USD, biggest first (ties: startup A-Z).
hints: WHERE keeps only matching rows: amount_usd >= 50000000.
ORDER BY amount_usd DESC, startup.
SELECT startup, amount_usd FROM funding_rounds WHERE amount_usd >= 50000000 ORDER BY amount_usd DESC, startup;

levels.title: Count what's missing
levels.story: An auditor always asks: how much of this data is unknown?
levels.task: How many rounds have no disclosed amount (amount_usd is NULL)? Return one column: undisclosed.
hints: NULL is not a value, so '= NULL' never matches. Use IS NULL.
COUNT(*) counts the remaining rows.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS undisclosed FROM funding_rounds WHERE amount_usd IS NULL;

cases.title: Funding Forensics
cases.tagline: Reported rounds don't add up. Audit the startup funding ledger before the annual report ships.
brief: The research desk publishes a yearly 'State of Indian Startups' report built from this funding ledger.
The ledger was frozen on 2020-01-22, yet the numbers keep shifting: some rounds are counted twice, city names come in a dozen spellings and a few entries look backdated.
Before the report goes to print, prove every number with SQL.

levels.title: Time travellers
levels.story: A round can't happen after the books were closed. Someone typed entries from the future.
levels.task: The ledger was frozen on 2020-01-22. List every round dated after that day. Return round_id, startup, deal_date.
hints: Dates are stored as ISO text (YYYY-MM-DD), so they compare correctly as strings.
Filter with WHERE deal_date > '2020-01-22'.
SELECT round_id, startup, deal_date FROM funding_rounds WHERE deal_date > '2020-01-22';

levels.title: Bengaluru by any other name
levels.story: The report says Mumbai beat Bengaluru. It didn't - Bengaluru was split across spellings.
levels.task: How many rounds are filed under Bengaluru, whatever the spelling? Count rows whose city_raw contains 'bangalore' or 'bengaluru' in any letter case. Return one column: rounds.
hints: LOWER(city_raw) makes the comparison case-insensitive.
Use LIKE '%bangalore%' OR LIKE '%bengaluru%'.
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rounds FROM funding_rounds WHERE LOWER(city_raw) LIKE '%bangalore%' OR LOWER(city_raw) LIKE '%bengaluru%';

levels.title: Double-booked rounds
levels.story: Totals are inflated. Somebody re-filed the same cheque with a slightly different name.
levels.task: Find rounds filed more than once: same startup (ignore case and surrounding spaces), same deal_date and same non-NULL amount_usd. Return startup_key (LOWER(TRIM(startup))), deal_date, amount_usd, copies.
hints: Group by the normalised name, the date and the amount.
Keep only groups with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, and skip NULL amounts.
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(startup)) AS startup_key, deal_date, amount_usd, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM funding_rounds WHERE amount_usd IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

levels.title: Biggest cheque of each year
levels.story: The report's headline chart: the record round of every year.
levels.task: For every year, find the single largest disclosed round (ties: lowest round_id). Return year (as text 'YYYY'), startup, amount_usd - sorted by year.
hints: strftime('%Y', deal_date) extracts the year.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY year ORDER BY amount_usd DESC, round_id) numbers rounds inside each year.

WITH r AS (SELECT strftime('%Y', deal_date) AS year, startup, amount_usd, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY strftime('%Y', deal_date) ORDER BY amount_usd DESC, round_id) AS rn FROM funding_rounds WHERE amount_usd IS NOT NULL AND deal_date IS NOT NULL) SELECT year, startup, amount_usd FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY year;

levels.title: Who writes the most cheques?
levels.story: The desk wants a 'most active investors' table - from the linked table, not by eyeballing text.
levels.task: Using round_investors, list the 5 investors that appear in the most rounds (ties: alphabetical). Return investor, rounds - most active first.
hints: round_investors has one row per investor per round.
GROUP BY investor, then ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC, investor and LIMIT 5.
SELECT investor, COUNT(*) AS rounds FROM round_investors GROUP BY investor ORDER BY rounds DESC, investor LIMIT 5;

levels.title: Teleporting riders
levels.story: Nobody rides a scooter through city traffic at highway speed. These timestamps were edited.
levels.task: Find orders whose implied speed is above 80 km/h (distance_km per delivery hour). Return order_id, platform, speed_kmh rounded to 1 decimal.
hints: Speed = distance / time. delivery_min is minutes, so divide by 60.0 to get hours.
ROUND(distance_km / (delivery_min / 60.0), 1) and filter on the unrounded value in WHERE.
SELECT order_id, platform, ROUND(distance_km / (delivery_min / 60.0), 1) AS speed_kmh FROM orders WHERE distance_km / (delivery_min / 60.0) > 80;

levels.title: Promise vs reality
levels.story: Marketing says '10 minutes'. Let the data say how often that is true.
levels.task: For each platform, what share of orders took longer than its promised_min? Return platform, orders, late_pct (percentage, 1 decimal) - worst first, ties by platform.
hints: JOIN orders to platforms on platform.
AVG(CASE WHEN delivery_min > promised_min THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) * 100 gives a percentage.

SELECT o.platform, COUNT(*) AS orders, ROUND(100.0 * AVG(CASE WHEN o.delivery_min > p.promised_min THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 1) AS late_pct FROM orders o JOIN platforms p ON p.platform = o.platform GROUP BY o.platform ORDER BY late_pct DESC, o.platform;

levels.title: Paid twice
levels.story: Incentives are paid per order. Per order means once.
levels.task: Some orders received more than one rider payout. Return order_id, payouts, total_paid (sum of amount, 2 decimals) for every such order.
hints: Group rider_payouts by order_id.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps the duplicates.
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS payouts, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS total_paid FROM rider_payouts GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

levels.title: Fastest app in every city
levels.story: The board wants one slide: who actually wins each city.
levels.task: In each city, which platform has the lowest average delivery time? Only count platforms with at least 20 orders in that city and ignore orders with no city; ties by platform name. Return city, platform, avg_min (1 decimal) sorted by city.
hints: First aggregate per (city, platform) with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20.
Then RANK or ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY avg, platform) and keep rank 1.

WITH s AS (SELECT city, platform, AVG(delivery_min) AS a FROM orders WHERE city IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city, platform HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20), r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY a, platform) AS rn FROM s) SELECT city, platform, ROUND(a, 1) AS avg_min FROM r WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY city;

levels.title: Ghost stock
levels.story: Sales are lost on items that are sitting on the shelf.
levels.task: List products marked out_of_stock = 1 that still have available_qty > 0. Return sku_id, name, available_qty.
hints: Two conditions joined with AND.
WHERE out_of_stock = 1 AND available_qty > 0
SELECT sku_id, name, available_qty FROM products WHERE out_of_stock = 1 AND available_qty > 0;

levels.title: Discounts that don't add up
levels.story: An advertised discount is a promise. Check the maths.
levels.task: Find products where selling_price differs from mrp * (100 - discount_pct) / 100 by more than 2 rupees. Return sku_id, mrp, discount_pct, selling_price.
hints: Compute the expected price from mrp and discount_pct.
ABS(actual - expected) > 2
SELECT sku_id, mrp, discount_pct, selling_price FROM products WHERE ABS(selling_price - mrp * (100 - discount_pct) / 100.0) > 2;

levels.title: Stock value by aisle
levels.story: Finance needs the money sitting in every aisle.
levels.task: For in-stock products (out_of_stock = 0), compute stock value = selling_price * available_qty per category. Return aisle_no, category, stock_value (2 decimals) - highest value first.
hints: JOIN products to categories to get aisle_no.
SUM(selling_price * available_qty) per category.

SELECT c.aisle_no, p.category, ROUND(SUM(p.selling_price * p.available_qty), 2) AS stock_value FROM products p JOIN categories c ON c.category = p.category WHERE p.out_of_stock = 0 GROUP BY c.aisle_no, p.category ORDER BY stock_value DESC;

levels.title: Same product, two prices

levels.task: Find products listed more than once in the same category with the same name and weight but different selling prices. Return category, name, weight_g, min_price, max_price.

HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT selling_price) > 1

levels.title: The riskiest hour
levels.story: Fraudsters keep office hours too. Find theirs.
levels.task: Which hour of the day (0-23) has the highest fraud rate among hours with at least 50 transactions? Return hour (integer), txns, fraud_rate_pct (2 decimals). One row.
hints: CAST(strftime('%H', ts) AS INTEGER) gives the hour.
AVG(fraud_flag) * 100 is the rate. HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50, ORDER BY rate DESC LIMIT 1.

SELECT CAST(strftime('%H', ts) AS INTEGER) AS hour, COUNT(*) AS txns, ROUND(100.0 * AVG(fraud_flag), 2) AS fraud_rate_pct FROM transactions GROUP BY hour HAVING COUNT(*) >= 50 ORDER BY fraud_rate_pct DESC, hour LIMIT 1;

levels.title: Leakiest corridors
levels.story: Money moves along corridors. Follow it.
levels.task: Top 3 sender_bank -> receiver_bank pairs by total amount of fraud-flagged transactions. Return sender_bank, receiver_bank, fraud_amount (2 decimals) - largest first.
hints: Filter fraud_flag = 1 first.
GROUP BY both bank columns, ORDER BY the sum DESC, LIMIT 3.
SELECT sender_bank, receiver_bank, ROUND(SUM(amount), 2) AS fraud_amount FROM transactions WHERE fraud_flag = 1 GROUP BY sender_bank, receiver_bank ORDER BY fraud_amount DESC LIMIT 3;

levels.title: Midnight whales
levels.story: The model watches small, noisy payments. Who watches the big quiet ones?
levels.task: List successful transfers above INR 50,000 made between 00:00 and 04:59 that were NOT flagged. Return txn_id, ts, amount.
hints: Hour 00-04 means strftime('%H', ts) < '05'.
Combine status = 'SUCCESS', fraud_flag = 0, amount > 50000.
SELECT txn_id, ts, amount FROM transactions WHERE status = 'SUCCESS' AND fraud_flag = 0 AND amount > 50000 AND strftime('%H', ts) < '05';

levels.title: Public vs private banks
levels.story: The audit committee wants one table for the slide deck.
levels.task: Compare fraud rates for senders from public-sector and private banks. Return bank_type ('private' or 'public'), txns, fraud_rate_pct (2 decimals).
hints: JOIN transactions to banks on sender_bank = bank.
CASE WHEN b.is_private = 1 THEN 'private' ELSE 'public' END

SELECT CASE WHEN b.is_private = 1 THEN 'private' ELSE 'public' END AS bank_type, COUNT(*) AS txns, ROUND(100.0 * AVG(t.fraud_flag), 2) AS fraud_rate_pct FROM transactions t JOIN banks b ON b.bank = t.sender_bank GROUP BY bank_type;

levels.title: Paid after leaving
levels.story: Once someone leaves, the salary stops. Unless it doesn't.
levels.task: List salary payments for a month that starts after the employee's exit_date. Return pay_id, emp_id, pay_month.
hints: JOIN payroll to employees.
A month 'YYYY-MM' starts on pay_month || '-01'. Compare that with exit_date.
SELECT p.pay_id, p.emp_id, p.pay_month FROM payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.emp_id = p.emp_id WHERE e.exit_date IS NOT NULL AND p.pay_month || '-01' > e.exit_date;

levels.title: One account, two salaries
levels.story: Classic ghost-employee pattern: a fake hire paid into a real person's account.
levels.task: Find bank accounts that receive salary for more than one employee. Return bank_account, employees.
hints: Group the employee master by bank_account.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT bank_account, COUNT(*) AS employees FROM employees GROUP BY bank_account HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

levels.title: The 2x payslip
levels.story: Bonuses go through a different system. A payslip should never double.
levels.task: Find payments where net_pay is more than 1.5 times the employee's monthly_income. Return pay_id, emp_id, net_pay, monthly_income.
hints: JOIN to employees to get monthly_income.
WHERE p.net_pay > 1.5 * e.monthly_income
SELECT p.pay_id, p.emp_id, p.net_pay, e.monthly_income FROM payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.emp_id = p.emp_id WHERE p.net_pay > 1.5 * e.monthly_income;

levels.title: Leak league table
levels.story: The CFO wants to know which department to talk to first.
levels.task: Rank departments by money paid after exit (the payments from level 1). Return department, cost_centre, leaked (2 decimals), leak_rank (RANK, 1 = biggest) - sorted by leak_rank, ties by department.
hints: Reuse the level-1 filter and SUM(net_pay) per department.
RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(p.net_pay) DESC) works directly in a grouped query.

SELECT e.department, d.cost_centre, ROUND(SUM(p.net_pay), 2) AS leaked, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(p.net_pay) DESC) AS leak_rank FROM payroll p JOIN employees e ON e.emp_id = p.emp_id JOIN departments d ON d.department = e.department WHERE e.exit_date IS NOT NULL AND p.pay_month || '-01' > e.exit_date GROUP BY e.department, d.cost_centre ORDER BY leak_rank;
